####################
THE INSTRUCTION / REGISTER:
CSRRWI

THE RULE:
CSRRWI obtains the XLEN-bit value to write to the CSR by zero-extending the 5-bit unsigned immediate field (uimm[4:0]) encoded in the rs1 field.

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:
##########
INSTRUCTION: CSRRWI
FORMAT: csrrwi rd, csr, zimm5
SUMMARY: CSRRWI writes the targeted CSR with an XLEN‑bit value formed by zero‑extending the 5‑bit immediate in the rs1 field, affecting all writable fields and their defined side‑effects. If rd ≠ x0, the instruction atomically reads the CSR, zero‑extends the old value to XLEN, and writes it to rd; if rd = x0, the CSR is written but no read or read‑side‑effects occur. The operation is subject to the normal privilege and access‑control checks for CSR writes. The instruction performs an atomic read‑modify‑write, or a write‑only when rd = x0.
##########
####################

The operation is subject to the normal privilege and access‑control checks for CSR writes. The instruction performs an atomic read‑modify‑write, or a write‑only when rd = x0.

THE INSTRUCTION / REGISTER:
SFENCE.VMA

THE RULE:
Changing satp.MODE from Bare to other modes and vice versa takes effect immediately, without the need to execute an SFENCE.VMA instruction.

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:
##########
INSTRUCTION: SFENCE.VMA
FORMAT: sfence.vma rs1, rs2
SUMMARY: SFENCE.VMA is a supervisor fence that flushes address‑translation structures; its encoding fixes funct3 to 000 and rd to x0, and rs1 optionally supplies a virtual address, which if invalid makes the instruction a no‑op. Execution is allowed only in S‑mode when mstatus.TVM=0; otherwise an illegal‑instruction exception is raised, while any use in U‑mode is illegal and in VS/VU modes a virtual‑instruction trap (exception code 22) is taken when hstatus.VTVM=1 or privilege is insufficient. The instruction follows the same permission checks and exception behavior as SINVAL.VMA, and virtual‑instruction traps write mtval/stval with the same value as an illegal‑instruction trap. No other exceptions are generated.

REGISTER: satp
CSR ADDRESS: 0x180
FIELDS: 63..60=MODE, 59..44=ASID, 43..0=PPN
MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: HS-mode
SUMMARY: The satp CSR controls supervisor virtual‑memory translation by holding a MODE field that selects the translation scheme (or Bare), an ASID field identifying the address space, and a PPN field pointing to the root page‑table physical page. MODE is read‑only zero when the implementation does not support any translation mode; otherwise it is a WARL field, ASID is writable up to the implementation‑defined ASIDLEN bits, and PPN is writable only when a supported MODE is selected. The register is readable and writable in S‑mode unless the mstatus TVM bit is set, in which case any S‑mode read, write, or execution of SFENCE.VMA/SINVAL.VMA causes an illegal‑instruction exception; M‑mode (and HS‑mode) may always access it, while U‑mode accesses are illegal. Writes of an unsupported MODE are ignored, and changes to MODE or ASID take effect immediately without requiring SFENCE.VMA or imposing ordering constraints on page‑table updates.
##########

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:

INSTRUCTION: SFENCE.VMA
FORMAT: sfence.vma rs1, rs2
SUMMARY: SFENCE.VMA is a supervisor fence that flushes address‑translation structures; its encoding fixes funct3 to 000 and rd to x0, and rs1 optionally supplies a virtual address, which if invalid makes the instruction a no‑op. Execution is allowed only in S‑mode when mstatus.TVM=0; otherwise an illegal‑instruction exception is raised, while any use in U‑mode is illegal and in VS/VU modes a virtual‑instruction trap (exception code 22) is taken when hstatus.VTVM=1 or privilege is insufficient. The instruction follows the same permission checks and exception behavior as SINVAL.VMA, and virtual‑instruction traps write mtval/stval with the same value as an illegal‑instruction trap. No other exceptions are generated.

REGISTER: mstatus
CSR ADDRESS: 0x300
FIELDS: 63..63=SD, 42..42=MDT, 41..41=MPELP, 39..39=MPV, 38..38=GVA, 37..37=MBE, 36..36=SBE, 35..34=SXL, 33..32=UXL, 23..23=SPELP, 22..22=TSR, 21..21=TW, 20..20=TVM, 19..19=MXR, 18..18=SUM, 17..17=MPRV, 16..15=XS, 14..13=FS, 12..11=MPP, 10..9=VS, 8..8=SPP, 7..7=MPIE, 6..6=UBE, 5..5=SPIE, 3..3=MIE, 1..1=SIE
MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: M-mode
SUMMARY: The mstatus CSR holds the machine‑mode architectural state, including global interrupt enables, current and previous privilege modes (MPP, MPP, MPIE, MIE, etc.), virtualization controls (V, MPV, MPRV), memory‑access modifiers (MXR, SUM, TSR, TVM, TW), endianness fields (MBE, SBE, UBE), XLEN configuration (SXL, UXL), and the dirty‑state bits for floating‑point, vector, and other extensions (FS, VS, XS) summarized by the read‑only SD bit. It is readable and writable only in machine mode; any access from a lower privilege and any attempt to execute or access vector or floating‑point instructions or CSRs when the corresponding VS or FS field is Off also raise an illegal‑instruction exception. Executing an instruction that can modify extension state automatically changes the relevant status field from Initial or Clean to Dirty, and a Dirty VS or FS forces SD = 1 (otherwise SD reflects any dirty extension). Trap entry and return instructions (xRET, MRET, SRET) update the privilege‑mode fields, interrupt‑enable bits, and virtualization fields as defined, while bits such as TSR, TVM, and TW impose additional legality restrictions on SRET, satp access, and user‑mode instruction fetches.

INSTRUCTION: SFENCE.VMA
FORMAT: sfence.vma rs1, rs2
SUMMARY: SFENCE.VMA is a supervisor fence that flushes address‑translation structures; its encoding fixes funct3 to 000 and rd to x0, and rs1 optionally supplies a virtual address, which if invalid makes the instruction a no‑op. Execution is allowed only in S‑mode when mstatus.TVM=0; otherwise an illegal‑instruction exception is raised, while any use in U‑mode is illegal and in VS/VU modes a virtual‑instruction trap (exception code 22) is taken when hstatus.VTVM=1 or privilege is insufficient. The instruction follows the same permission checks and exception behavior as SINVAL.VMA, and virtual‑instruction traps write mtval/stval with the same value as an illegal‑instruction trap. No other exceptions are generated.

REGISTER: hstatus
CSR ADDRESS: 0x600
FIELDS: 63..50=WPRI, 49..48=HUPMM, 47..34=WPRI, 33..32=VSXL, 31..23=WPRI, 22..22=VTSR, 21..21=VTW, 20..20=VTVM, 19..18=WPRI, 17..12=VGEIN, 11..10=WPRI, 9..9=HU, 8..8=SPVP, 7..7=SPV, 6..6=GVA, 5..5=VSBE, 4..0=WPRI

No other exceptions are generated.

THE INSTRUCTION / REGISTER:
VLE32FF.V

THE RULE:
VLE32FF.V MUST execute as a regular load except that it will only take a trap caused by a synchronous exception on element 0.

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:
##########
INSTRUCTION: VLE32FF.V
FORMAT: vle32ff.v vd, (rs1), vm
SUMMARY: VLE32FF.V is a 32‑bit element vector load that uses the architectural vector length register (vl) to bound the number of elements fetched and the vector‑start register (vstart) to record the current element index. A synchronous exception on element 0 causes an immediate trap without modifying vl, whereas an exception on any later element does not trap and instead truncates vl to that element's index. If an interrupt or a debug data‑watchpoint occurs on an element beyond the first, vl is left unchanged and vstart (or the debug trap) is updated so execution can resume correctly. The instruction obeys the normal load privilege checks and requires no special access permissions.
##########
####################

SUMMARY: VLE32FF.V is a 32‑bit element vector load that uses the architectural vector length register (vl) to bound the number of elements fetched and the vector‑start register (vstart) to record the current element index. A synchronous exception on element 0 causes an immediate trap without modifying vl, whereas an exception on any later element does not trap and instead truncates vl to that element's index. If an interrupt or a debug data‑watchpoint occurs on an element beyond the first, vl is left unchanged and vstart (or the debug trap) is updated so execution can resume correctly. The instruction obeys the normal load privilege checks and requires no special access permissions.

FIELDS: 63..0=VALUE

INSTRUCTION: VLE32FF.V
FORMAT: vle32ff.v vd, (rs1), vm
SUMMARY: VLE32FF.V is a 32‑bit element vector load that uses the architectural vector length register (vl) to bound the number of elements fetched and the vector‑start register (vstart) to record the current element index. A synchronous exception on element 0 causes an immediate trap without modifying vl, whereas an exception on any later element does not trap and instead truncates vl to that element's index. If an interrupt or a debug data‑watchpoint occurs on an element beyond the first, vl is left unchanged and vstart (or the debug trap) is updated so execution can resume correctly. The instruction obeys the normal load privilege checks and requires no special access permissions.

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. The RLB bit determines whether locked PMP rules can be modified, and when MML is set PMP entries become sticky and mode‑specific (M‑mode‑only or S/U‑mode‑only), causing illegal‑instruction or access‑fault exceptions for disallowed accesses. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. The RLB bit determines whether locked PMP rules can be modified, and when MML is set PMP entries become sticky and mode‑specific (M‑mode‑only or S/U‑mode‑only), causing illegal‑instruction or access‑fault exceptions for disallowed accesses. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. The RLB bit determines whether locked PMP rules can be modified, and when MML is set PMP entries become sticky and mode‑specific (M‑mode‑only or S/U‑mode‑only), causing illegal‑instruction or access‑fault exceptions for disallowed accesses. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. The RLB bit determines whether locked PMP rules can be modified, and when MML is set PMP entries become sticky and mode‑specific (M‑mode‑only or S/U‑mode‑only), causing illegal‑instruction or access‑fault exceptions for disallowed accesses. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:

FIELDS: 63..34=WPRI, 33..32=PMM, 31..11=WPRI, 10..10=MLPE, 9..9=SSEED, 8..8=USEED, 7..3=WPRI, 2..2=RLB, 1..1=MMWP, 0..0=MML

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. The RLB bit determines whether locked PMP rules can be modified, and when MML is set PMP entries become sticky and mode‑specific (M‑mode‑only or S/U‑mode‑only), causing illegal‑instruction or access‑fault exceptions for disallowed accesses. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. The RLB bit determines whether locked PMP rules can be modified, and when MML is set PMP entries become sticky and mode‑specific (M‑mode‑only or S/U‑mode‑only), causing illegal‑instruction or access‑fault exceptions for disallowed accesses. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: M-mode
SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. The RLB bit determines whether locked PMP rules can be modified, and when MML is set PMP entries become sticky and mode‑specific (M‑mode‑only or S/U‑mode‑only), causing illegal‑instruction or access‑fault exceptions for disallowed accesses. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. The RLB bit determines whether locked PMP rules can be modified, and when MML is set PMP entries become sticky and mode‑specific (M‑mode‑only or S/U‑mode‑only), causing illegal‑instruction or access‑fault exceptions for disallowed accesses. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. The RLB bit determines whether locked PMP rules can be modified, and when MML is set PMP entries become sticky and mode‑specific (M‑mode‑only or S/U‑mode‑only), causing illegal‑instruction or access‑fault exceptions for disallowed accesses. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:
##########
REGISTER: mseccfg
CSR ADDRESS: 0x747
FIELDS: 63..34=WPRI, 33..32=PMM, 31..11=WPRI, 10..10=MLPE, 9..9=SSEED, 8..8=USEED, 7..3=WPRI, 2..2=RLB, 1..1=MMWP, 0..0=MML
MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: M-mode
SUMMARY: The mseccfg CSR is a machine‑mode 64‑bit read/write register that configures security controls such as enabling user or supervisor access to the seed CSR (USEED, SSEED), PMP locking and mode‑specific behavior (RLB, MML, MMWP), pointer‑masking (PMM), and extension enable bits (MLPE). In Machine mode the register imposes no restrictions on seed CSR accesses, whereas in User or Supervisor modes a read‑write seed CSR is allowed only if the corresponding USEED or SSEED bit is set; any other seed‑CSR access or access from lower privilege modes triggers an illegal‑instruction exception. The RLB bit determines whether locked PMP rules can be modified, and when MML is set PMP entries become sticky and mode‑specific (M‑mode‑only or S/U‑mode‑only), causing illegal‑instruction or access‑fault exceptions for disallowed accesses. Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).
##########

Pointer‑masking is controlled by the PMM field, MLPE enables Zicfilp in M‑mode, and writes to undefined fields or attempts to read/write mseccfg from non‑machine modes also raise illegal‑instruction exceptions (mcause = 2).

SUMMARY: The mstatus CSR holds the machine‑mode architectural state, including global interrupt enables, current and previous privilege modes (MPP, MPP, MPIE, MIE, etc.), virtualization controls (V, MPV, MPRV), memory‑access modifiers (MXR, SUM, TSR, TVM, TW), endianness fields (MBE, SBE, UBE), XLEN configuration (SXL, UXL), and the dirty‑state bits for floating‑point, vector, and other extensions (FS, VS, XS) summarized by the read‑only SD bit. It is readable and writable only in machine mode; any access from a lower privilege and any attempt to execute or access vector or floating‑point instructions or CSRs when the corresponding VS or FS field is Off also raise an illegal‑instruction exception. Executing an instruction that can modify extension state automatically changes the relevant status field from Initial or Clean to Dirty, and a Dirty VS or FS forces SD = 1 (otherwise SD reflects any dirty extension). Trap entry and return instructions (xRET, MRET, SRET) update the privilege‑mode fields, interrupt‑enable bits, and virtualization fields as defined, while bits such as TSR, TVM, and TW impose additional legality restrictions on SRET, satp access, and user‑mode instruction fetches.

REGISTER: satp
CSR ADDRESS: 0x180
FIELDS: 63..60=MODE, 59..44=ASID, 43..0=PPN
MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: HS-mode
SUMMARY: The satp CSR controls supervisor virtual‑memory translation by holding a MODE field that selects the translation scheme (or Bare), an ASID field identifying the address space, and a PPN field pointing to the root page‑table physical page. MODE is read‑only zero when the implementation does not support any translation mode; otherwise it is a WARL field, ASID is writable up to the implementation‑defined ASIDLEN bits, and PPN is writable only when a supported MODE is selected. The register is readable and writable in S‑mode unless the mstatus TVM bit is set, in which case any S‑mode read, write, or execution of SFENCE.VMA/SINVAL.VMA causes an illegal‑instruction exception; M‑mode (and HS‑mode) may always access it, while U‑mode accesses are illegal. Writes of an unsupported MODE are ignored, and changes to MODE or ASID take effect immediately without requiring SFENCE.VMA or imposing ordering constraints on page‑table updates.

Executing an instruction that can modify extension state automatically changes the relevant status field from Initial or Clean to Dirty, and a Dirty VS or FS forces SD = 1 (otherwise SD reflects any dirty extension). Trap entry and return instructions (xRET, MRET, SRET) update the privilege‑mode fields, interrupt‑enable bits, and virtualization fields as defined, while bits such as TSR, TVM, and TW impose additional legality restrictions on SRET, satp access, and user‑mode instruction fetches.

mstatus

THE RULE:
When the TVM bit in mstatus is 1, attempts to write the satp CSR while executing in S-mode raise an illegal-instruction exception.

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:
##########
REGISTER: mstatus
CSR ADDRESS: 0x300
FIELDS: 63..63=SD, 42..42=MDT, 41..41=MPELP, 39..39=MPV, 38..38=GVA, 37..37=MBE, 36..36=SBE, 35..34=SXL, 33..32=UXL, 23..23=SPELP, 22..22=TSR, 21..21=TW, 20..20=TVM, 19..19=MXR, 18..18=SUM, 17..17=MPRV, 16..15=XS, 14..13=FS, 12..11=MPP, 10..9=VS, 8..8=SPP, 7..7=MPIE, 6..6=UBE, 5..5=SPIE, 3..3=MIE, 1..1=SIE
MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: M-mode
SUMMARY: The mstatus CSR holds the machine‑mode architectural state, including global interrupt enables, current and previous privilege modes (MPP, MPP, MPIE, MIE, etc.), virtualization controls (V, MPV, MPRV), memory‑access modifiers (MXR, SUM, TSR, TVM, TW), endianness fields (MBE, SBE, UBE), XLEN configuration (SXL, UXL), and the dirty‑state bits for floating‑point, vector, and other extensions (FS, VS, XS) summarized by the read‑only SD bit. It is readable and writable only in machine mode; any access from a lower privilege and any attempt to execute or access vector or floating‑point instructions or CSRs when the corresponding VS or FS field is Off also raise an illegal‑instruction exception. Executing an instruction that can modify extension state automatically changes the relevant status field from Initial or Clean to Dirty, and a Dirty VS or FS forces SD = 1 (otherwise SD reflects any dirty extension). Trap entry and return instructions (xRET, MRET, SRET) update the privilege‑mode fields, interrupt‑enable bits, and virtualization fields as defined, while bits such as TSR, TVM, and TW impose additional legality restrictions on SRET, satp access, and user‑mode instruction fetches.

REGISTER: satp
CSR ADDRESS: 0x180
FIELDS: 63..60=MODE, 59..44=ASID, 43..0=PPN
MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: HS-mode
SUMMARY: The satp CSR controls supervisor virtual‑memory translation by holding a MODE field that selects the translation scheme (or Bare), an ASID field identifying the address space, and a PPN field pointing to the root page‑table physical page. MODE is read‑only zero when the implementation does not support any translation mode; otherwise it is a WARL field, ASID is writable up to the implementation‑defined ASIDLEN bits, and PPN is writable only when a supported MODE is selected. The register is readable and writable in S‑mode unless the mstatus TVM bit is set, in which case any S‑mode read, write, or execution of SFENCE.VMA/SINVAL.VMA causes an illegal‑instruction exception; M‑mode (and HS‑mode) may always access it, while U‑mode accesses are illegal. Writes of an unsupported MODE are ignored, and changes to MODE or ASID take effect immediately without requiring SFENCE.VMA or imposing ordering constraints on page‑table updates.

SUMMARY: SFENCE.VMA is a supervisor fence that flushes address‑translation structures; its encoding fixes funct3 to 000 and rd to x0, and rs1 optionally supplies a virtual address, which if invalid makes the instruction a no‑op. Execution is allowed only in S‑mode when mstatus.TVM=0; otherwise an illegal‑instruction exception is raised, while any use in U‑mode is illegal and in VS/VU modes a virtual‑instruction trap (exception code 22) is taken when hstatus.VTVM=1 or privilege is insufficient. The instruction follows the same permission checks and exception behavior as SINVAL.VMA, and virtual‑instruction traps write mtval/stval with the same value as an illegal‑instruction trap. No other exceptions are generated.

SUMMARY: The satp CSR controls supervisor virtual‑memory translation by holding a MODE field that selects the translation scheme (or Bare), an ASID field identifying the address space, and a PPN field pointing to the root page‑table physical page. MODE is read‑only zero when the implementation does not support any translation mode; otherwise it is a WARL field, ASID is writable up to the implementation‑defined ASIDLEN bits, and PPN is writable only when a supported MODE is selected. The register is readable and writable in S‑mode unless the mstatus TVM bit is set, in which case any S‑mode read, write, or execution of SFENCE.VMA/SINVAL.VMA causes an illegal‑instruction exception; M‑mode (and HS‑mode) may always access it, while U‑mode accesses are illegal. Writes of an unsupported MODE are ignored, and changes to MODE or ASID take effect immediately without requiring SFENCE.VMA or imposing ordering constraints on page‑table updates.

THE INSTRUCTION / REGISTER:
mstatus

THE RULE:
When the TVM bit in mstatus is 0, attempts to execute an SFENCE.VMA instruction while executing in S-mode are permitted.

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:
##########
REGISTER: mstatus
CSR ADDRESS: 0x300
FIELDS: 63..63=SD, 42..42=MDT, 41..41=MPELP, 39..39=MPV, 38..38=GVA, 37..37=MBE, 36..36=SBE, 35..34=SXL, 33..32=UXL, 23..23=SPELP, 22..22=TSR, 21..21=TW, 20..20=TVM, 19..19=MXR, 18..18=SUM, 17..17=MPRV, 16..15=XS, 14..13=FS, 12..11=MPP, 10..9=VS, 8..8=SPP, 7..7=MPIE, 6..6=UBE, 5..5=SPIE, 3..3=MIE, 1..1=SIE
MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: M-mode
SUMMARY: The mstatus CSR holds the machine‑mode architectural state, including global interrupt enables, current and previous privilege modes (MPP, MPP, MPIE, MIE, etc.), virtualization controls (V, MPV, MPRV), memory‑access modifiers (MXR, SUM, TSR, TVM, TW), endianness fields (MBE, SBE, UBE), XLEN configuration (SXL, UXL), and the dirty‑state bits for floating‑point, vector, and other extensions (FS, VS, XS) summarized by the read‑only SD bit. It is readable and writable only in machine mode; any access from a lower privilege and any attempt to execute or access vector or floating‑point instructions or CSRs when the corresponding VS or FS field is Off also raise an illegal‑instruction exception. Executing an instruction that can modify extension state automatically changes the relevant status field from Initial or Clean to Dirty, and a Dirty VS or FS forces SD = 1 (otherwise SD reflects any dirty extension). Trap entry and return instructions (xRET, MRET, SRET) update the privilege‑mode fields, interrupt‑enable bits, and virtualization fields as defined, while bits such as TSR, TVM, and TW impose additional legality restrictions on SRET, satp access, and user‑mode instruction fetches.

INSTRUCTION: SFENCE.VMA
FORMAT: sfence.vma rs1, rs2
SUMMARY: SFENCE.VMA is a supervisor fence that flushes address‑translation structures; its encoding fixes funct3 to 000 and rd to x0, and rs1 optionally supplies a virtual address, which if invalid makes the instruction a no‑op. Execution is allowed only in S‑mode when mstatus.TVM=0; otherwise an illegal‑instruction exception is raised, while any use in U‑mode is illegal and in VS/VU modes a virtual‑instruction trap (exception code 22) is taken when hstatus.VTVM=1 or privilege is insufficient. The instruction follows the same permission checks and exception behavior as SINVAL.VMA, and virtual‑instruction traps write mtval/stval with the same value as an illegal‑instruction trap. No other exceptions are generated.

Trap entry and return instructions (xRET, MRET, SRET) update the privilege‑mode fields, interrupt‑enable bits, and virtualization fields as defined, while bits such as TSR, TVM, and TW impose additional legality restrictions on SRET, satp access, and user‑mode instruction fetches.

THE RULE:
If the FS, VS, or XS field in mstatus is Initial, executing an instruction that may modify the corresponding state causes the field to transition to Dirty.

THE BACKGROUND INFORMATION:
##########
REGISTER: mstatus
CSR ADDRESS: 0x300
FIELDS: 63..63=SD, 42..42=MDT, 41..41=MPELP, 39..39=MPV, 38..38=GVA, 37..37=MBE, 36..36=SBE, 35..34=SXL, 33..32=UXL, 23..23=SPELP, 22..22=TSR, 21..21=TW, 20..20=TVM, 19..19=MXR, 18..18=SUM, 17..17=MPRV, 16..15=XS, 14..13=FS, 12..11=MPP, 10..9=VS, 8..8=SPP, 7..7=MPIE, 6..6=UBE, 5..5=SPIE, 3..3=MIE, 1..1=SIE
MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: M-mode
SUMMARY: The mstatus CSR holds the machine‑mode architectural state, including global interrupt enables, current and previous privilege modes (MPP, MPP, MPIE, MIE, etc.), virtualization controls (V, MPV, MPRV), memory‑access modifiers (MXR, SUM, TSR, TVM, TW), endianness fields (MBE, SBE, UBE), XLEN configuration (SXL, UXL), and the dirty‑state bits for floating‑point, vector, and other extensions (FS, VS, XS) summarized by the read‑only SD bit. It is readable and writable only in machine mode; any access from a lower privilege and any attempt to execute or access vector or floating‑point instructions or CSRs when the corresponding VS or FS field is Off also raise an illegal‑instruction exception. Executing an instruction that can modify extension state automatically changes the relevant status field from Initial or Clean to Dirty, and a Dirty VS or FS forces SD = 1 (otherwise SD reflects any dirty extension). Trap entry and return instructions (xRET, MRET, SRET) update the privilege‑mode fields, interrupt‑enable bits, and virtualization fields as defined, while bits such as TSR, TVM, and TW impose additional legality restrictions on SRET, satp access, and user‑mode instruction fetches.

Executing an instruction that can modify extension state automatically changes the relevant status field from Initial or Clean to Dirty, and a Dirty VS or FS forces SD = 1 (otherwise SD reflects any dirty extension). Trap entry and return instructions (xRET, MRET, SRET) update the privilege‑mode fields, interrupt‑enable bits, and virtualization fields as defined, while bits such as TSR, TVM, and TW impose additional legality restrictions on SRET, satp access, and user‑mode instruction fetches.

SUMMARY: The satp CSR controls supervisor virtual‑memory translation by holding a MODE field that selects the translation scheme (or Bare), an ASID field identifying the address space, and a PPN field pointing to the root page‑table physical page. MODE is read‑only zero when the implementation does not support any translation mode; otherwise it is a WARL field, ASID is writable up to the implementation‑defined ASIDLEN bits, and PPN is writable only when a supported MODE is selected. The register is readable and writable in S‑mode unless the mstatus TVM bit is set, in which case any S‑mode read, write, or execution of SFENCE.VMA/SINVAL.VMA causes an illegal‑instruction exception; M‑mode (and HS‑mode) may always access it, while U‑mode accesses are illegal. Writes of an unsupported MODE are ignored, and changes to MODE or ASID take effect immediately without requiring SFENCE.VMA or imposing ordering constraints on page‑table updates.

MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: HS-mode
SUMMARY: The satp CSR controls supervisor virtual‑memory translation by holding a MODE field that selects the translation scheme (or Bare), an ASID field identifying the address space, and a PPN field pointing to the root page‑table physical page. MODE is read‑only zero when the implementation does not support any translation mode; otherwise it is a WARL field, ASID is writable up to the implementation‑defined ASIDLEN bits, and PPN is writable only when a supported MODE is selected. The register is readable and writable in S‑mode unless the mstatus TVM bit is set, in which case any S‑mode read, write, or execution of SFENCE.VMA/SINVAL.VMA causes an illegal‑instruction exception; M‑mode (and HS‑mode) may always access it, while U‑mode accesses are illegal. Writes of an unsupported MODE are ignored, and changes to MODE or ASID take effect immediately without requiring SFENCE.VMA or imposing ordering constraints on page‑table updates.

Writes of an unsupported MODE are ignored, and changes to MODE or ASID take effect immediately without requiring SFENCE.VMA or imposing ordering constraints on page‑table updates.

FIELDS: 63..60=MODE, 59..44=ASID, 43..0=PPN
MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: HS-mode
SUMMARY: The satp CSR controls supervisor virtual‑memory translation by holding a MODE field that selects the translation scheme (or Bare), an ASID field identifying the address space, and a PPN field pointing to the root page‑table physical page. MODE is read‑only zero when the implementation does not support any translation mode; otherwise it is a WARL field, ASID is writable up to the implementation‑defined ASIDLEN bits, and PPN is writable only when a supported MODE is selected. The register is readable and writable in S‑mode unless the mstatus TVM bit is set, in which case any S‑mode read, write, or execution of SFENCE.VMA/SINVAL.VMA causes an illegal‑instruction exception; M‑mode (and HS‑mode) may always access it, while U‑mode accesses are illegal. Writes of an unsupported MODE are ignored, and changes to MODE or ASID take effect immediately without requiring SFENCE.VMA or imposing ordering constraints on page‑table updates.

MINIMUM PRIVILEGE REQUIRED TO ACCESS THIS REGISTER: HS-mode
SUMMARY: The satp CSR controls supervisor virtual‑memory translation by holding a MODE field that selects the translation scheme (or Bare), an ASID field identifying the address space, and a PPN field pointing to the root page‑table physical page. MODE is read‑only zero when the implementation does not support any translation mode; otherwise it is a WARL field, ASID is writable up to the implementation‑defined ASIDLEN bits, and PPN is writable only when a supported MODE is selected. The register is readable and writable in S‑mode unless the mstatus TVM bit is set, in which case any S‑mode read, write, or execution of SFENCE.VMA/SINVAL.VMA causes an illegal‑instruction exception; M‑mode (and HS‑mode) may always access it, while U‑mode accesses are illegal. Writes of an unsupported MODE are ignored, and changes to MODE or ASID take effect immediately without requiring SFENCE.VMA or imposing ordering constraints on page‑table updates.
